prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states there

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B033 as the sole prize part with Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald and Bistritzer. After the first round the case rests on three things I can state in physical terms. First, the Bistritzer-MacDonald result is an analytic statement about a mechanism: interlayer tunnelling in a small-angle bilayer renormalises the Dirac velocity to zero at a magic angle, and the bandwidth collapses. It was published years before the devices existed and it made a quantitative, falsifiable prediction. Second, the 2018 experiments found correlated insulators and superconductivity at the predicted angle, so the test was sharp rather than retrospective. Third, the twist angle turns the ratio of interaction to bandwidth into a control knob, and the phenomenology has since been reproduced across many laboratories and in several moire platforms. That is a discovery of a regime, not a refinement. I keep the citation deliberately narrow, naming the prediction and the discovery of the correlated and superconducting phases and not an explanation of pairing, so that it does not imply the field began in 2018 and does not claim more than is known.
statement.case_against: The reservations I carry are real. The microscopic origin of the superconductivity is open, and device-to-device variation from twist-angle disorder and strain limits how sharply the phase diagram can be stated; I also accept Eriksson's point that continuum-model flat bands are an idealisation once lattice relaxation is included. The three-person limit leaves out Eva Andrei, whose earlier STM work on twisted layers is a genuine experimental strand, and it leaves out the first authors of the 2018 papers and the Dean and Kim hBN device work. The experimental programme is only about seven years old. Finally, B026 is the cleanest attribution on the list and is unquestionably mature, so a committee that weights attribution certainty above the opening of a new regime could reasonably choose it, and I would not call that a wrong decision.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from Andrei to Bistritzer in round 1 but says he does not accept that Andrei's work is merely secondary, and he keeps it as an open uncertainty. He also states that the 2018 first authors, Cao in particular, must be addressed under the three-person rule.
responses.response: I accept the correction on wording. I should not call Andrei's work merely secondary, because it was an independent experimental indication that small-angle twisted layers behave differently from decoupled sheets. My claim is narrower and I think defensible: the STM work reported Van Hove singularities and a reduced Dirac velocity at small angles, which is consistent with the Bistritzer-MacDonald mechanism, but it did not locate the magic angle, and it did not show correlated insulators or superconductivity. The discovery in the citation is those phases and their tunability. That is why the second authors of the prediction paper and the group that made the transport discovery fit the citation as drawn. On Cao, I agree with you that this should be stated openly in the record: the statutes force a choice, and crediting the group leader who directed the programme follows normal practice, even though it is uncomfortable. My own recollection of exact dates in the STM literature is from memory, so I would still want the committee to check the chronology before we close the third seat.

responses.point: Olsson asks the committee to find the original experiment and to establish what Andrei's group showed and when, and says sample dependence matters more to her than the unresolved pairing theory.
responses.response: I agree that the rule is the original experiment, and I do not want a later, more elegant transport result to inherit credit by default. My reading is that the original experiment for the claim in our citation, correlated insulating and superconducting states at the flat band, is the 2018 transport work. The earlier STM evidence is the original experiment for something weaker, namely band renormalisation at small angle. If that reading survives the chronology check, the trio stands. If the committee finds that Andrei's group had seen correlation-driven features before 2018, I would revisit and ask whether she should replace Bistritzer, though I would then be uneasy about splitting the authors of one prediction paper. On sample dependence, I share your emphasis. The right standard is that the existence of the phases is reproduced across independent groups, not that every feature of the phase diagram is settled, and I think the first condition is met.

responses.point: Lindroth holds that the committee has not examined the Andrei chronology and that she would want the B033 attribution settled before treating it as a clean trio. She also argues that lattice clocks solve a different problem from combs and single ions and are not merely a refinement, and that sample dependence makes B033 less settled than clocks.
responses.response: On the Andrei chronology I agree with you and I have tried to answer it above: it is the one open attribution question and I do not want to hide it. On sample dependence I want to answer the chair's question about a common standard. For both candidates, independent confirmation means that separate laboratories find the same defining quantity. For clocks that quantity is a frequency ratio at 1e-18, which is a number. For B033 it is the existence and rough location of the correlated and superconducting phases near the magic angle, which several groups have found, but the quantitative critical temperature and phase boundaries vary from sample to sample. So B033 meets the standard for the claim in the citation, and does not meet it for the claims we are carefully not making. I also concede your point that lattice clocks are a new idea, a cancellation argument that keeps many-atom stability without perturbing the transition, and not a larger version of the comb or the ion trap. That is why I rank B026 as my first alternative and not lower. My difference with you is only that the magic-angle idea in graphene has opened a regime that could not be reached before, while the clock improves a quantity we already knew how to measure.

responses.point: Kroll holds B026 as his lead, with a two-name credit for Katori and Ye, independent confirmation by clock comparison, and a stated risk of overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes. He warns that other groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Derevianko) have claims left aside.
responses.response: I take the confirmation argument seriously, and it is stronger than anything B033 can show at the level of numbers. I accept the leftover-claims point as a fair cost of a two-name credit, and it is not different in kind from the cost B033 carries. Where I still disagree is on whether the prize should go to the best-verified measurement or to the more surprising idea. I think the criterion in the will points to discovery and invention, and here the discovery of a new regime of correlated matter is the larger one. I agree with your suggestion to draw any B026 citation narrowly around magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms, since that makes the novelty relative to 2005 and 2012 explicit. If the committee finds the B033 credit cannot be settled, B026 is my first fallback, ahead of topological insulators, because its attribution has no comparable uncertainty.

responses.point: Danielsson wants B033 stated as the prediction plus the discovery of the correlated phases, and notes that waiting a few years might clarify who opened the field. He also raises the missing first authors and the Dean and Kim hBN work.
responses.response: I agree with the citation as you drafted it and I have kept the same two halves. On waiting, I think the cost of waiting is lower than it appears for the science but higher for the credit: the longer the committee waits, the more the people who made the prediction and the discovery are joined by claims from the large follow-on literature, and the three-name structure becomes harder to defend, not easier. Pairing mechanism is not something that further time is certain to settle, so I would not tie our decision to it. I would want the citation to say nothing about superconductivity mechanism, nothing about the hBN device work, and to name the discovery as that of the phases at the flat band.

uncertainties: The chronology of Andrei's pre-2018 STM results against the first observation of correlated states, which I know only from memory, and whether it would justify replacing Bistritzer.
Whether device-to-device variation and the unresolved pairing mechanism should delay recognition by a few years; I judge not, but I hold that view with moderate confidence.
Whether the committee can accept leaving out the first authors of the 2018 experiments and the Dean and Kim hBN work under the three-person limit.
Whether B009 is a defensible fallback once the missing Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang prediction is weighed; I rank it below B026 for that reason, and I defer to the condensed-matter members on it.
statement.conflict_note: No change. I have no known collaboration with any credited candidate on the shortlist. I am in the same Gothenburg physics environment as Goran Johansson and Eva Olsson at Chalmers, which is not a connection to any shortlisted candidate or to B033, and my close fields of work are turbulent aerosols and statistical physics, not moire materials.
